concepts.name: A three-minute pitch: problem, design, decision, metrics, change
Presenting one hard decision: context, options, consequences
What you would change: reflection that invites follow-ups

questions.prompt: "Walk me through your best project in three minutes." Which opening is strongest?

choices.text: "I used LangGraph, pgvector, FastAPI, Redis and Docker, all deployed on a single VPS."
"Our support team triaged tickets by hand for six hours a day, so I built a routing agent."
"It started in March, when I first read about agents, and then in April I began building..."
"The hardest part was a race condition in the checkpointer that took me a week to find."

questions.explanation: Amazon asks for answers that tell a story with a beginning, middle and end, starting with just enough situation to show why it mattered. The second option names the problem, who had it, and a number. A list of tools, a timeline or a bug has no problem for the design to solve.

sources.title: Interview Loop
sources.claim: Amazon asks that each answer have a beginning, middle and end, opening with just enough situation to show the big picture and what made it challenging.

questions.prompt: Your recorded pitch runs five minutes. What does Amazon suggest for balancing detail?

choices.text: Speak faster so all the detail fits into the time you have left
Drop the metrics, since the interviewer can ask for them later
Be concise but complete, then pause and ask if they want more
Skip the problem and start with the design, where the detail is

questions.explanation: Amazon's tips say to be clear and concise but include enough detail for a complete story, and suggest pausing after your answer to ask whether the interviewer wants more. Cutting the problem or the metrics removes the parts that make the design matter.

sources.title: Interview Loop
sources.claim: Amazon's tips say to be clear and concise while including enough detail for a complete story, then pause and ask if the interviewer wants more context.

questions.prompt: Your design section lists LangGraph, pgvector, FastAPI and Redis. What does Amazon's advice say is missing?

choices.text: A diagram showing how the components connect
The exact version number of each library you used
The names of the other libraries you tried first
The why behind each decision, not only the what

questions.explanation: Amazon's interview prep asks you to focus on the "what" and "how" of your work and also the "why" of your decisions. A list of tools says what, not why. One hard decision explained well is worth more than a full stack list.

sources.title: Interview prep for technical roles
sources.claim: Amazon's technical interview prep says interviews focus on the what and how of your experiences as well as the why of your decisions.

questions.prompt: In Michael Nygard's Architecture Decision Record format, which section must list the negative results of a decision as well as the positive ones?

choices.text: Consequences
Context
Decision
Status

questions.explanation: Nygard's Consequences section describes the situation after applying the decision, and says all consequences should be listed, not just the positive ones. Context describes the forces at play, Decision states the response ("We will..."), and Status says whether it is proposed, accepted, deprecated or superseded.

sources.title: Documenting Architecture Decisions
sources.claim: Nygard's Consequences section describes the resulting context and says all consequences should be listed, not just the positive ones.

questions.prompt: In about 30 seconds of your pitch, present one hard decision, such as pgvector vs a hosted vector database. Explain how you would structure it.

model_answer.summary: Use the shape of an architecture decision record: the forces at play, the options, the decision in active voice, and the consequences, including the cost you accepted.
key_points: Context: the forces that made it hard, such as data size, budget, latency or operations effort
The decision, stated actively: "I chose X"
Consequences, including the downside or trade-off you accepted
Evidence, such as a measurement, for why it was the right call

questions.explanation: Nygard's ADR format fits a spoken decision well, and its rule that consequences include the negatives is what makes the story believable. Interviewers probe trade-offs, so naming the downside yourself shows judgement. This repository's own `docs/adr/` uses the same idea.

sources.title: Documenting Architecture Decisions
sources.claim: Nygard's ADR has Context (forces at play), Decision (stated in active voice, "We will..."), Status and Consequences including negative ones.

retired.reason: Written Questions are legacy (ADR-0008): replaced by a multiple-select Question on the same Concept.

questions.prompt: Your agent API has a mean latency of 900 ms. Why should your pitch also give p95 or p99 latency?

choices.text: Percentiles are always lower than the mean, so they sound better
A mean can't be computed for streamed responses
Most requests can be fast while a long tail is much slower, and the mean hides that
Interviewers only accept the median (p50)

questions.explanation: Google's SRE book warns that averaging request latencies hides the fact that most requests can be fast while a long tail is much slower. Percentiles show the shape of the distribution: the median shows the typical case and p99 the bad cases. Percentiles can be higher or lower than the mean.

sources.title: Chapter 4 - Service Level Objectives
sources.claim: The SRE book warns that averaging request latencies can hide that most requests are fast while a long tail is much slower, and recommends percentiles.

questions.prompt: In a test run, 19 requests take 500 ms and one takes 10,500 ms. What are the mean and the median latency?

choices.text: Mean 1,000 ms, median 500 ms
Mean 500 ms, median 500 ms
Mean 1,025 ms, median 1,000 ms
Mean 10,500 ms, median 500 ms

questions.explanation: Mean = (19 × 500 + 10,500) / 20 = 20,000 / 20 = 1,000 ms. With 20 values sorted, the middle two are both 500 ms, so the median is 500 ms. One slow request doubles the mean while the median doesn't move, which is why you report percentiles alongside it.

sources.title: Chapter 4 - Service Level Objectives
sources.claim: The SRE book recommends looking at the latency distribution via percentiles such as the median rather than the mean, since an average hides the slow tail.

questions.prompt: Pick the metrics for a pitch about a RAG support bot and explain how you would state them so an interviewer believes them.

model_answer.summary: Give a before-and-after comparison, latency as percentiles, a quality score with how it was measured, and cost per request. Say how and on what each was measured.
key_points: Compare against a baseline: before vs after, or old vs new
Give latency as percentiles such as p50 and p95, not just the mean
Give a quality metric with how it was measured, such as an eval set and its size
Give cost per request (or per ticket)
Say how each number was measured, so it is a defined, checkable indicator

questions.explanation: The SRE book defines a service level indicator as a carefully defined quantitative measure, which is the standard a pitch metric should meet. Amazon asks for data and results to back up your story. A number with no baseline or method invites the follow-up "compared with what?"

sources.title: Chapter 4 - Service Level Objectives
sources.claim: The SRE book defines an SLI as a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of service, and recommends latency percentiles over averages.

sources.title: Interview Loop
sources.claim: Amazon asks candidates to back up their story with data or results where possible.

retired.reason: Written Questions are legacy (ADR-0008): replaced by a multiple-select Question on the same Concept.

questions.prompt: The interviewer asks, "What would you change about your architecture now?" Which answer is best?

choices.text: "Nothing, honestly. It works well in production, so I wouldn't change anything about it."
"I'd rewrite it all in a newer framework, since that one is more popular with teams now."
"The client kept changing the requirements, so that was the real problem, not the architecture."
"I'd move retries to the worker; timeouts doubled cost in traces, though it adds a moving part."

questions.explanation: Amazon says it values self-awareness and a willingness to learn, and asks what you learned. The last option names a specific change, the evidence behind it and the trade-off. "Nothing" shows no reflection, a rewrite for popularity has no reason, and blaming the client avoids the question.

sources.title: Interview Loop
sources.claim: Amazon says it values authenticity, self-awareness and a willingness to learn, and asks what you learned.

sources.title: Documenting Architecture Decisions
sources.claim: Nygard's ADR format records consequences of a decision, including the negative ones.

questions.prompt: Explain why a three-minute pitch should end with what you would change, and what makes that part strong.

model_answer.summary: It shows reflection and self-awareness, the "what did you learn" part of a good story. It is strong when it names a specific change, ties it to evidence you saw, and states the trade-off, which leads into a follow-up you are ready for.
key_points: It shows reflection: what you learned and how you would grow (the extra R in STARR)
Interviewers value self-awareness over a perfect record
A strong answer names one specific change and the evidence behind it, such as a metric or trace
It states the trade-off of the change, which invites a follow-up question you have prepared for

questions.explanation: Amazon's Result guidance asks what you learned, and the Tech Interview Handbook's STARR adds reflection. This week's interview checks include "What would you change about your architecture now?", so the pitch rehearses that answer.

sources.title: Interview Loop
sources.claim: Amazon's Result guidance asks what you learned, and it values self-awareness over perfection.

sources.title: Behavioral interviews for Software Engineers: How to prepare | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: The handbook's STARR adds a final Reflection on what you learned and took away.

questions.prompt: Which elements make a difficult architecture decision explainable? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Describe the technical and business forces shaping the choice.
State the decision clearly in active language.
List only favorable consequences and hide accepted disadvantages.
Present the chosen technology without any context.
Explain both positive and negative consequences of the choice.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: ADR context captures the relevant forces. B: Correct: an explicit decision identifies what was chosen. C: Incorrect: negative and neutral effects matter to future readers. D: Incorrect: context explains why the choice made sense. E: Correct: consequences include all effects, not only benefits.

sources.title: Documenting Architecture Decisions
sources.claim: Nygard's ADR has Context (forces at play), Decision (stated in active voice, "We will..."), Status and Consequences including negative ones.

questions.prompt: Which metric statements make a project pitch more credible? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Report only mean latency because it always reveals the slow tail.
State defined quantitative measures and how they were obtained.
Use median and high-percentile latency to describe the distribution.
Back claims of impact with specific data or results.
Treat p95 latency as proof that no request can be slower.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: averages can hide tail latency and its changes. B: Correct: a carefully defined indicator is interpretable and checkable. C: Correct: percentiles distinguish typical from tail experience. D: Correct: Amazon recommends specific data demonstrating impact. E: Incorrect: roughly five percent of observations can exceed p95.

sources.title: Chapter 4 - Service Level Objectives
sources.claim: The SRE book defines an SLI as a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of service, and recommends latency percentiles over averages.

sources.title: Amazon interview preparation: recruiter tips
sources.claim: Recruiters recommend STAR, specific personal contributions and data, and discussing failures, learning and self-reflection.

questions.prompt: Which reflections make the end of a project pitch useful? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Describe a specific lesson learned from the experience.
Claim the project was flawless so no improvement is possible.
Explain how you would act differently based on that lesson.
Omit every mistake because self-criticism always harms an interview.
Connect the reflection to how you grew or improved.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: STARR adds reflection on what was learned. B: Incorrect: a perfect-record claim prevents meaningful reflection. C: Correct: the Result discussion can include steps taken to improve. D: Incorrect: Amazon welcomes self-reflection and growth from failures. E: Correct: reflection communicates learning beyond the outcome.

sources.claim: The handbook's STARR adds a final Reflection on what you learned and took away.

sources.claim: Recruiters recommend STAR, specific personal contributions and data, and discussing failures, learning and self-reflection.
